newsitem.title: UK: EMU, regulation vie at London derivatives jamboree.
newsitem.headline: EMU, regulation vie at London derivatives jamboree.

text.p: The likely impact of a single European currency has pushed regulation into second place on the priority list for derivatives players as they prepare for London's main industry conference this week.

The fourth international derivatives conference will be held here on Wednesday and Thursday. Speakers include Howard Davies, deputy governor of the Bank of England, and representatives from leading exchanges.

While politicians have the luxury of battling over who is in or out and how to meet criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU), companies cannot afford to wait until the 1999 starting bell.

"People are focused on whether they can get their businesses up and running in time," said Chris Taylor, partner in global capital markets and Treasury group at Price Waterhouse. "And perhaps more importantly, on whether they will actually have a business under the euro environment."
Analysts said it was proving difficult for companies to imagine the post-EMU world -- and even harder to admit that there will be losers.

In the derivatives industry in particular, where the number of products will be slashed as bond and interest rate contracts from those countries within EMU are replaced with euro denominated assets, analysts said competition among companies and exchanges will be fierce.

The declining product range will reignite competitive forces, said John Gubert, head of group securities services at HSBC group in London. From a product point of view there will be fundamental change, and it could mean structural change as well.

Practical issues such as the reprogramming of computers to understand the new euro, are compounded by the impending millennium which may send some computers haywire. Older machines, so-called legacy systems, recognise only the last two digits of the year, so will interpret the year 2000 as the year 1900.
But Gubert said companies are less in the dark now about the likely shape of the technological future and have started to get their houses in order.
There is certainly more awareness about the problems, and a lot of planning is underway, he said. The question is whether organisations are far enough down the road. The answer is no.

And no derivatives debate would be complete without regulation rearing its head. In the post-Barings world, where companies are constantly demanded to make derivatives use as safe as possible, industry players said the issue remains firmly on the agenda.

Also, Chancellor Gordon Brown unveiled plans last month to transfer responsibility for supervising banks from the Bank of England to a strengthened Securities and Investment Board (SIB), and market participants are keen for clues on how it will operate.

The new SIB will regulate all banks, securities firms and insurance companies. While firm control would be welcomed, analysts said an organisation with too severe a reputation could be a threat to innovative products, and also to the niche market trading which has helped build London's financial strength.

Well have to see how it works out, but just bundling regulation under the super-SIB doesnt mean everything will be alright, said Jeremy Wagener, director general of the Association of Corporate Treasurers.
In some ways things have swung too far. Its time we went back to a more caveat emptor approach, to encourage consumers to behave more responsibly.
If super-SIB reinforces a focus on constantly filling in forms, then well have a situation where no one can do any business.
